uncited: **Footprint Table:** A 2D lookup table storing the analytically integrated kernel function along a traversing ray.

The source explicitly states that traditional splatting summed kernels within slices parallel to the viewing direction (implied by the contrast with image-aligned splatting and the mention of brightness variations in animated viewing), whereas Mueller's method (image-aligned splatting) processes kernels within slabs aligned parallel to the image plane. The source confirms this method eliminates brightness variations and allows for variable interval distances (DVRI interval distance ∆s).

Axis-aligned sheet buffers (in basic splatting) introduce "popping" artifacts; Mueller's image-aligned approach reduces this but requires dynamic occlusion map updates [S4, S7].

The evidence in Source [S4] explicitly states that the 'axis-aligned sheet buffer approach introduces “popping” artifacts' and that 'Mueller et al. aligned the sheet buffers parallel to the image plane' (image-aligned) to address issues. Source [S7] confirms that Mueller's method involves 'image-aligned splatting' and details the use of a 'dynamically computed screen occlusion map' with 'dynamic construction... requires a convolution operation after each sheet-buffer composite'. Thus, all components of the claim (axis-aligned causes popping, Mueller's image-aligned approach reduces this, and it requires dynamic occlusion map updates) are supported by the provided texts.

It solves the computational cost of 3D convolution by pre-integrating the kernel along the viewing ray to create a 2D footprint table, which is then rasterized onto the screen [S1, S3, S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the method solves computational cost by pre-integrating the kernel along the viewing ray to create a 2D footprint table, which is then rasterized. Source [S1] explicitly defines the footprint function $F(x, y)$ as the integral of the kernel $h$ along the $u$ axis (parallel to the viewing ray) and describes generating a 'footprint table' from this integral. Source [S3] confirms this by stating one can 'pre-integrate' the kernel and store the result in a 'lookup-table called the kernel footprint,' and then 'rasterize the footprint to the screen.' Source [S5] reiterates the definition of the footprint function as the integral along the viewing ray. All factual components of the claim are present in the provided evidence.
supported
